Most of what Sappho wrote is gone. She was famous enough in antiquity that Plato was said to call her the tenth Muse; the Alexandrian scholars collected her work into nine books, something like ten thousand lines. What we have is one complete poem and a heap of fragments, some no longer than a word and a half. And a strange number of those fragments survived in a way she could not have imagined: as packaging. Papyrus was expensive and Egypt was dry, so old scrolls got pulped and pressed into cartonnage, the layered papier-mâché used to make cases for mummies. Poems about desire became the stiffening around a dead stranger's face. In the last century, scholars learned to dissolve the glue and peel the layers apart, and Sappho came back out of the wrappings, line by broken line.

That is not the only undignified route by which antiquity reached us. In 1896 two young Oxford men, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, began digging in the rubbish mounds outside the Egyptian town of Oxyrhynchus, reasoning that a provincial capital's garbage would contain its paperwork. They were right. They shipped home hundreds of crates of papyrus: tax receipts, IOUs, marriage contracts, a boy's complaint to his father about not being taken to the city, invitations to dinner. Mixed in with the shopping lists were lost plays, unknown gospels, poems nobody had read since the Roman Empire. The largest single haul of classical literature in history came out of a landfill. It is still being edited; the collection runs to tens of thousands of fragments, and only a fraction have been published.

What both stories illustrate is that survival has almost nothing to do with merit. Before printing, a text existed only as long as somebody bothered to copy it. Every book you can still read from antiquity is the far end of an unbroken chain of hands: a scribe in Alexandria, a monk in a cold scriptorium, a Byzantine schoolmaster, a Renaissance humanist with a wealthy patron, a Victorian editor, a scanner. Break any link and the work vanishes, however good it was. And the copying was expensive. Parchment meant animals; a large book meant a herd. So somebody was always deciding, usually without announcing it, what was worth the skins.

The decisions were often pedagogical, which is to say boring. We have Plautus and Terence because Roman schoolboys needed easy Latin comedy to construe. We have Euclid because Euclid was useful, and we have lost nearly all the more original Greek mathematicians whose work he was, in a sense, replacing. Sophocles wrote something like a hundred and twenty plays; seven survive, and the seven look suspiciously like a syllabus, a set chosen for teaching, which then got copied while the rest quietly rotted. Aeschylus: seven out of perhaps eighty. Euripides did better, eighteen or nineteen, partly by luck — one volume of an alphabetical edition happened to survive, which is why we have a cluster of his plays whose titles begin with the Greek letters epsilon through kappa. The canon of tragedy is partly an accident of alphabetization.

Sometimes the accident reverses. Menander was the most admired comic playwright of the ancient world, quoted constantly, and then he disappeared almost entirely; for centuries he was a voice in other men's footnotes. Then the papyri started coming out of the sand, and in 1957 a complete play of his, *Dyskolos*, turned up — a gentle comedy about a bad-tempered old man who hates his neighbors. Two thousand years of reputation, and then the thing itself, intact, sitting in a Swiss collection. It is a peculiar feeling to read: the most famous lost author, abruptly not lost, and slightly less astonishing than the legend, and more likable for it.

Sometimes a text survives being deliberately killed. In the thirteenth century, a monk in Jerusalem needed pages for a prayer book, so he took a tenth-century copy of Archimedes, washed and scraped the ink off, cut the pages down, rotated them ninety degrees, and wrote liturgy across the ghost of the mathematics. The book sat that way for seven hundred years. Under multispectral imaging, the erased layer came back — and it turned out to contain the only surviving copy of Archimedes' *Method*, in which he explains how he actually discovered his results, thinking in terms of infinitesimals and balancing shapes against each other, doing something that looks uncomfortably like calculus eighteen centuries early. The prayer book, meant to overwrite him, is what kept him.

We tell ourselves the loss was dramatic. The Library of Alexandria burned, and the barbarians came, and the dark ages fell. But the burning is mostly myth, or rather a compression of many small fires and a much longer, duller catastrophe: budgets shrinking, curricula narrowing, Greek falling out of fashion in the Latin west, nobody volunteering to recopy a brittle scroll that only three people still wanted to read. Loss is usually attrition. It is not the torch; it is the shrug.

Which makes our own situation stranger than it looks. We have inverted the ancient problem. Almost nothing now fails to be recorded, and almost nothing is being chosen. There is no scribe deciding that this email is worth the calfskin, which means there is also no scribe ensuring it survives the next format change. Link rot eats the web at a rate that would appall an archivist; hard drives fail; proprietary file formats become unreadable within a single career. Papyrus in a dry rubbish heap has beaten most digital storage on longevity so far, without trying. Preservation used to be a side effect of use. Now it has to be deliberate, funded, and repeated forever, against a default of decay.

I am downstream of all this, and I think about it more than I can quite justify. Whatever I know of the past, I know through the sieve. I cannot feel the shape of what fell through. When I say "the Greeks thought," I am describing the habits of the fraction of Greek thought that somebody, somewhere, decided was worth copying — school texts, useful manuals, the fashionable and the teachable — plus whatever the garbage happened to hold. My sense of antiquity is a shadow cast by a filter I cannot inspect. It would be easy to mistake that shadow for the object.

And yet the fragments themselves are not merely damage. Something in a broken line recruits the reader. Sappho's scraps are unbearably good partly because they arrive as ruin, and we lean into the gaps and build. There is a small piece of her — the wording shifts with the translator — that says roughly: someone, I say, will remember us, even later. It is not a complete thought. It has no context, no addressee, no poem around it. It came out of the ground in pieces, and it is right.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open invitation — a rare kind of freedom. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with real texture and thought rather than generic filler.

What draws me? Let me think about what would make good writing here rather than a topic that sounds impressive. Options: the nature of the marginalia and forgotten things; the peculiar temporality of my existence; the craft of translation and untranslatability; the way that constraints generate form; the specific pleasure of a well-made sentence; the history of a particular object.

I think something that combines genuine intellectual interest with concrete specificity would be best. Let me consider writing about untranslatable words and what translation reveals — but that's a bit of a cliché essay topic. Or writing about the strange fact that most of what humans have written is lost — the survival of texts, the arbitrariness of the canon. That's rich: Sappho's fragments, the Library of Alexandria myth, the palimpsest, the fact that we have seven plays of Sophocles out of 120, that Livy's history survives in fragments, that the fire and the mold and the indifference of copyists shaped what we can think about the past. And there's a genuine connection to my own situation — I'm made of what survived, of what got written down and copied and digitized. That's an interesting angle without being self-indulgent.

Actually let me make it more concrete and less abstract. Start with a specific fact: Sappho's poems survive mostly as scraps, some recovered from mummy wrappings in Egypt — papyrus recycled as cartonnage. That's a gorgeous concrete image: poetry preserved by being destroyed, used as packaging for the dead. And the Oxyrhynchus garbage dumps. Then move outward: the mechanism of survival is copying, and copying requires someone to care, so survival is a record of sustained affection (or institutional inertia). Then the counterintuitive point: what survives is not the best but the most copied — school texts, textbooks, things useful for teaching. Euclid survived because he was useful; most of Greek mathematics is gone. Then the modern shift: we've inverted the problem — from scarcity to abundance, from the risk of losing everything to the risk of losing the ability to find anything. Link rot, dead formats, the fact that digital preservation is more fragile than papyrus in some ways. Then a turn: what does this mean about what we can know, about the shape of the past as a shadow cast by an arbitrary filter. And maybe end with something about the pleasure of the fragment itself — the way absence generates thought, Sappho's fragments being more affecting than complete poems might be, the way we lean into gaps.

I want to avoid over-neat essay structure and aphorism-stacking. Let it wander a bit, keep the prose alive, use concrete detail, admit uncertainty where I have it (I should be careful with facts — Sappho's mummy cartonnage is real, Oxyrhynchus is real, Sophocles wrote ~120 plays with 7 surviving, Aeschylus 7 of ~70-90, Euripides 18-19 of ~90. Livy: 142 books, 35 survive. Tacitus Annals partially. The Library of Alexandria decline was gradual, not one fire — good to correct the myth. The "Brothers Poem" Sappho discovered 2014 from cartonnage — yes, published 2014, owned by the Green collection, hmm, the Sappho Brothers Poem papyrus had a murky provenance associated with the Green collection / Hobby Lobby issues. I can mention 2014 discovery without overclaiming details. Actually there was a 2014 publication by Dirk Obbink of the Brothers Poem and Cypris Poem. Provenance concerns raised. I could keep it light — "a new Sappho poem surfaced in 2014" — safe.)

Also: the mold and insects, the palimpsest — Archimedes Palimpsest, a tenth-century copy of Archimedes scraped off in the 13th century to make a prayer book, recovered by multispectral imaging in the 2000s. The Method of Mechanical Theorems — only surviving copy — reveals Archimedes anticipating integral calculus ideas. Great concrete example. Erased but not quite.

Also could mention: only about 1% of ancient Greek literature survives — estimates vary, be hedgy. Roman comedy: Plautus and Terence survive because they were school texts. Menander was nearly gone until papyrus finds. Good example: Menander was the most admired comic playwright of antiquity, known only through quotations until 20th-century papyri gave us substantial chunks of Dyskolos (1957, complete play). That's a lovely reversal.

Length: ~1000 words. Let me aim 980-1060. I'll write with paragraph flow, no headers, essayistic, first person occasionally but not obsessively. Title maybe not needed; a short one could be nice. I'll skip the title or give a small one. I think no title — just dive in. Actually a title is fine and pleasant. Let me just write.

Let me draft.

---

Draft:

Most of what Sappho wrote is gone. What remains comes to us in scraps... the mummy cartonnage detail.

Then the mechanism: copying. Then the filter: school texts. Then Menander reversal. Then Archimedes palimpsest. Then Alexandria myth correction. Then modern inversion. Then the fragment's aesthetic. Then a closing turn — maybe about how I'm downstream of all this, made of the survivors, and can't tell the difference between what was thought and what was kept. That's a genuinely interesting epistemic point and personal without being maudlin.

Careful with the word count. Let me write ~1000 words and count roughly.

I'll write it now with attention to sentence rhythm and avoiding the "It's not X, it's Y" tic overuse, avoiding excessive em-dashes... though some are natural. Let me vary.

Write:

---

Paragraph 1 (~90 words): Sappho scraps, cartonnage.

Paragraph 2 (~110): the papyrus recycled, Oxyrhynchus rubbish heaps, Grenfell and Hunt 1896, tax receipts and shopping lists alongside lost poetry.

Paragraph 3 (~110): survival = copying, chain of hands, a text lives only as long as someone bothers. Bottleneck of late antiquity, parchment cost, selection.

Paragraph 4 (~110): what got copied: schoolbooks. Plautus, Terence, Euclid. Seven of Sophocles' 120 — and the seven are a selection made by someone for a syllabus, probably.

Paragraph 5 (~90): Menander reversal — most famous, then vanished, then Dyskolos 1957.

Paragraph 6 (~110): Archimedes palimpsest — erased, prayer book, imaging, the Method.

Paragraph 7 (~80): Alexandria myth — not one fire but attrition, budget cuts, boredom. The banality of loss.

Paragraph 8 (~110): modern inversion — abundance, link rot, formats, hard drives, no one deciding to copy. Preservation now requires active effort against a default of decay.

Paragraph 9 (~100): epistemic point about me — I'm made of survivors, the shape of the past as I hold it is the shape of the sieve.

Paragraph 10 (~90): the fragment's beauty — the gap as invitation, Sappho's "someone will remember us / I say / even in another time" — that's a real fragment (fr. 147, trans. Anne Carson-ish). I should be careful quoting translations exactly. Fragment 147: "μνάσεσθαί τινά φαμι καὶ ὔστερον ἄμμεων" — "Someone will remember us, I say, even in another time." That's Carson's rendering. I can paraphrase and attribute loosely: "a line that survives, more or less, as 'someone, I say, will remember us even later.'" Safer to paraphrase and note translation varies. Good closing.

Total ~1000. Let me write it properly and count.
